introduction: Choose a checked clock reading from Dan Robinson's original dashcam upload. Each button sets the path, warning and radar viewers to that historical time and selects the corresponding video position.
method: These are discrete clock observations, read from paused frames in the original upload. They are not a continuous synchronization of every frame. A video offset is recorded separately from the CDT clock printed on the footage; CDT is converted to UTC by adding five hours. Browser seeking can land on a nearby frame. Compare the visible clock before making a precise comparison. No camera coordinates, viewing bearings, wind measurements or fatal impact locations are inferred from these samples.
coverage: Only the listed paused samples and the creator description were checked. No full video or audio audit has been completed. The space between samples remains unregistered. Playing the original video leaves the historical map paused, so unreviewed frames do not acquire an invented event time.

guide.title: A video has two clocks
guide.text: Elapsed player time tells you where you are in an upload. The clock printed inside a shot may tell you when it happened. Cuts, replays and altered playback speed can break a single offset between the two. Here, each checked dashcam moment has its own correspondence. The intervening footage remains available to watch without claiming it is continuously synchronized.

guide.title: The camera is not the tornado
guide.text: A camera position describes the observer. A bearing describes where the camera points, not the distance to the visible feature. The El Reno Survey Project recommends recognizable landmarks, accurate clocks and location records because all three help register a view. Its guidance also warns that wide-angle distortion complicates interpretation. A source photograph without that information remains valuable, but cannot establish a precise funnel location by itself.

sources.label: El Reno Survey Project field methods

guide.title: A visible edge is not a safe boundary
guide.text: Rain, spray and the viewing angle can obscure what the circulation is doing. In Robinson's sampled views, water on the windshield and low contrast hide much of the surrounding scene. A clear outline in one photograph does not establish the full width of damaging winds. The official path and documented damage must be read alongside the view.

guide.title: Damage rating and radar measurement
guide.text: The Enhanced Fujita scale estimates wind intensity from damage indicators and degrees of damage. Radar measurements describe sampled air motion with their own height, resolution and timing. They answer related questions with different evidence. This exhibit retains the final EF3 damage rating while discussing the mobile-radar research separately; an old EF5 video title does not change the final rating.

sources.label: NWS explanation of the EF scale

guide.title: A landmark does not identify a person
guide.text: A road sign can help locate a camera. A matching vehicle shape is a lead, not a confirmed identity. Establishing a fatal impact requires more than a nearby timestamp or a recovery photograph. The remembrance map labels the kind of location the evidence supports and keeps unsupported coordinates out of the record.

guide.title: Bring the original record
guide.text: The most useful contribution is an original source with the relevant timestamp, visible landmarks and an explanation of the clock. Keep the camera operator's name and the upload version with the observation. A popular repost can remove those details. Research findings and disagreements belong beside the evidence, so a later correction can be traced.
